text: Tools and Technology Efficacy and Precision of Fecal Genotyping to Estimate Coyote Abundance

Questions concerning the effects on other wildlife species by coyotes (Canis latrans) in recently colonized areas, including the southeastern United States, continue to receive attention in the literature. Coyote abundance estimates, achieved via genetic sampling of feces, can be useful in answering such questions. However, rapid degradation of fecal DNA in humid subtropical climates, like that of the southeastern United States, may limit the efficacy of the technique. To evaluate this hypothesis, we collected and analyzed 434 suspected coyote scats from February 2010 to April 2012 on 2 sites in central Georgia, USA. We quantified seasonal and comprehensive genotyping success, and the effect of sampling effort on precision of closed population abundance estimates. We successfully species-typed 316 (73%) scats, 219 (69%) of which belonged to coyotes. Of those, 136 (62%) yielded multilocus genotypes. The seasonal probability of genotyping a scat ranged from 0.53 to 0.71. Scats collected during spring were more likely to yield consensus genotypes, but the overall effect of season on genotyping success was minimal. The median CV for model-averaged b N (i.e., coyote abundance) using the complete data set was relatively precise (<15%). Precision of abundance estimates decreased with decreasing sampling effort, but CV values remained <20% with up to a 25% reduction in effort. Our findings related to genotyping success demonstrate noninvasive genetic sampling of feces is a promising technique for estimating coyote abundance in humid subtropical climates. Combined with our results regarding sampling effort, these findings can aid in designing surveys capable of achieving desired objectives in similar environments.

The distribution of coyotes (Canis latrans) has expanded during the past 2 centuries to include all of North America except for the far northeastern regions of Canada (Bekoff and Gese 2003). Coyotes colonized areas east of the Mississippi River in the United States along a northern and a southern front. The northern front moved across the Great Lakes region and into northeastern states, while the southern front moved across the southeastern United States (Moore andParker 1992, Parker 1995), perhaps aided by human translocation (Hill et al. 1987). Since then, coyotes have rapidly increased in number throughout the southeastern United States (Kilgo et al. 2010).
Coyotes are medium-sized, generalist predators with a broad diet. In areas where large canids or felids are absent, coyotes may suppress populations of smaller carnivores, thereby increasing abundance and diversity of songbirds and rodents (Levi and Wilmers 2012). Evidence also suggests coyotes are responsible for the majority of neonatal whitetailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus) mortality in the Southeast (Saalfeld and Ditchkoff 2007, Jackson 2011, Kilgo et al. 2012, McCoy et al. 2013, Chitwood et al. 2015, Nelson et al. 2015). Given the ability of coyotes to affect a wide variety of taxa including white-tailed deer, the region's most pursued and economically important game species (U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service 2011), both managers and researchers are interested in improving understanding of coyote ecology to inform management decisions.
Estimating abundance and demographic parameters is often a first and necessary step in adapting wildlifemanagement strategies following colonization by a new species (Bozarth et al. 2015). To account for the elusive nature of coyotes, several researchers have used DNA collected from coyote scats deposited along roads and trails to noninvasively mark and recapture individuals, allowing for estimation of abundance or other parameters of interest. This technique was used to estimate coyote abundance in the states of Virginia (Bozarth et al. 2015, Morin et al. 2016), California (Kohn et al. 1999, Fedriani et al. 2001), New York (Kays et al. 2008), and Alaska, USA (Prugh et al. 2005).
However, fecal genotyping is not without limitations. Fecal samples usually contain small quantities of low-quality DNA, which may result in failure to obtain a PCR product for subsequent analysis; thereby, decreasing the effective sample size or leading to genotyping errors (Taberlet et al. 1999). Genotyping errors can bias abundance estimates by leading to either creation of false alleles or an inability to distinguish distinct individuals (Taberlet et al. 1996, Mills et al. 2000, Waits and Leberg 2000, Marucco et al. 2011). Hence, much effort has been devoted to understanding how factors such as sample age and environmental conditions affect DNA degradation and, thus, sample quality (Farrell et al. 2000, Nsubuga et al. 2004, Piggott 2004, Murphy et al. 2007, Santini et al. 2007, Lonsinger et al. 2015). In general, genotyping success is greater when only the freshest scats are sampled during cooler, drier periods, or in areas with cold, xeric climates (Farrell et al. 2000, Lucchini et al. 2002, Nsubuga et al. 2004, Piggott 2004, Murphy et al. 2007, Santini et al. 2007).
Researchers can reduce sample age by increasing sampling frequency or sampling only those scats subjectively evaluated as fresh. However, collecting scats during cool, dry periods is difficult in the humid subtropical climate of the Southeast where interest in estimating coyote abundance is high because of their relatively recent colonization. Therefore, our objective was to assess the feasibility of using fecal genotyping for this purpose in the Southeast and areas with similar climates to provide researchers and managers with guidelines for making decisions regarding use of the technique prior to its implementation. We collected coyote scats for approximately 2 years on 2 sites in central Georgia, USA, and quantified seasonal and comprehensive genotyping success, as well as the effect of sampling effort on precision of closed population abundance estimates. We predicted our overall success rates would be lower than those for colder or more xeric climates, but would be greatest during autumn, because this season on our study areas most closely resembles optimal conditions for preservation of fecal DNA.

We conducted research on portions of B.F. Grant (BFG) and Cedar Creek (CC) wildlife management areas in Putnam County, Georgia (Fig. 1). These areas were separated by approximately 8 km at their closest point. The terrain was gently rolling and elevation ranged from 120 m to 180 m. B. F. Grant was owned by the University of Georgia and CC was part of the Oconee National Forest. Central Georgia had a humid, subtropical climate. During summer, high temperatures averaged approximately 328 C and overnight lows ranged from 168 to 218 C. During winter, high temperatures ranged from 108 to 168 C, with lows averaging approximately 28 C. Temperatures during spring and autumn were more variable. However, the first frost usually occurred in mid-November and the last frost was typically in mid-to late-March. Annual rainfall amounts ranged from 114 cm to 127 cm. The driest months were typically September and October and the wettest month was March (National Weather Service 2015).

section: methods scat collection and genetic analysis
text: We collected putative coyote scats approximately weekly on each study area during February 2010-April 2012 along permanently identified survey routes that consisted of unpaved roads and trails. Survey routes totaled 28 km on BFG and 20 km on CC and traversed blocks of approximately 2,000 ha within the interior of each site. We used published criteria of size, shape, contents, and odor to subjectively differentiate coyote scats from those deposited by other species (Murie 1974). Because the quality of DNA was significantly lower in wolf (C. lupus) scats >3 days old, we preserved samples of only those scats estimated to be 3 days old (based on moisture content and degree of decomposition) for genetic confirmation of species of origin and microsatellite genotyping for individual coyote identification (Santini et al. 2007). We collected approximately 3 mL (i.e., size of a small grape) of fecal matter from the outside edges of each scat in the field and placed the sample into a 15-mL polystyrene centrifuge tube filled with 9 mL of 95% EtOH (Stenglein et al. 2010). We labeled each tube with a unique identification number and the date of collection. The portion of each scat remaining after subsampling was removed from the survey route. We sent preserved scats from Georgia to the University of California Davis Veterinary Genetics Laboratory for analysis. We extracted DNA from feces using the Qiagen QiaAmp Stool Kit (Qiagen, Valencia, CA, USA). We used mitochondrial sequencing to determine species using the cytochrome b fragment amplified by primers RF14724 and RF15149 (Perrine et al. 2007), followed by BLAST search in GenBank. Specifically, we performed polymerase chain reactions (PCRs) in 25-mL total volumes consisting of 2 mL of DNA extract, 2.5 mL of 10Â PCR buffer, 2.0 mL of 10 mM dNTPs, 1.5 mL of 25 mM MgCl2, 1 mL each of 10 mM forward and reverse primers, 0.3 mL of 5 U/mL Taq and water to make up the remainder of the volume. The PCR thermal profile was 948 C for 3 min; 45 cycles of 948 C for 30 s, 508 C for 30 s, and 728 C for 45 s; followed by a 10-min extension at 728 C. We sequenced each product from the forward primer using ABI Big Dye terminator sequencing reagents following manufacturer's guidelines and sequenced products on an ABI 3730 capillary sequencer (Applied Biosystems, Foster City, CA). Our criterion for accepting species-level matches during BLAST search was >98% homology to a single species. We used 12 microsatellites and a sex marker (based on X and Y chromosome paralogs of the amelogenin gene) genotyped in 2 multiplex reactions to determine individual genotypes and genetic sex (An et al. 2010). We fluorescently labeled forward primers (6FAM, VIC, NED, PET; Applied Biosystems) and performed reactions as described previously by An et al. ( 2010) except that we organized loci into multiplexes as follows: multiplex 1 incorporated AHTh171, CPH18, CXX-468, CXX-602, REN54P11, and the sex marker; multiplex 2 incorporated AHT137, AHT142, CXX-279, CXX-374, INU055, REN162C04, and REN169O18. We conducted PCRs using the Qiagen multiplex kit according to the manufacturer's recommended protocols (including Q-solution). We electrophoresed PCR products on an ABI 3730 capillary sequencer (Applied Biosystems) and scored alleles relative to an internal size standard, Genescan 500 LIZ (Applied Biosystems), using STRand software (Toonen and Hughes 2001). We replicated all fecal genotypes at least twice. We considered high-quality samples (i.e., all loci represented in !1 replicate and !7 loci amplified in the other) complete. By using 2 independent genotypes, the probability of a false homozygote due to 2 dropouts of the same allele was small (one-half the square of the probability of a single allelic dropout, approx. 4%), but not negligible. Therefore, rather than assume 100% accuracy of final genotypes (as is standard in studies that use smaller numbers of loci; e.g., 6), our approach was to accommodate genotyping error by using a sufficient number of loci of sufficient polymorphism to detect erroneous genotype mismatches probabilistically with high confidence (see Lounsberry et al. 2015 for details). Nevertheless, we replicated genotypes falling below the threshold of 7 amplified loci up to 5 additional times (3-7 total replicates) and included only those with no missing loci in further analyses (Lounsberry et al. 2015). We divided the number of dropouts by the number of successful replicates for each heterozygous locus (as determined from consensus genotypes) to calculate the allelic dropout rate. We used GenAlEx 6.5 (Peakall andSmouse 2006, 2012) to calculate the probability of individual identity and probability of identity for siblings for each locus and increasing combinations of the 12 loci (Waits et al. 2001). We used the AlleleMatch package in R to perform a pairwise genotypematching analysis resulting in creation of composite genotypes for unique individuals (Galpern et al. 2012, R Core Team 2014).

Following genotyping, we analyzed these data to determine the probability of successfully genotyping scats during each season and explore the effects of varying sampling effort on precision of abundance estimates. We defined seasons as spring (Mar-May), summer (Jun-Aug), autumn (Sep-Nov), and winter (Dec-Feb). We used logistic regression in Program R to determine the probability of a scat yielding a consensus genotype within each season (R Core Team 2014). First, we constructed the model with season as the explanatory variable with the binary response of success as the response variable. We considered parameter estimates for seasons with 95% confidence intervals not overlapping zero informative. We also used the predict function with the model to calculate the estimated probability of genotyping success and associated 95% confidence limits for each season. Because these estimates were on the logit scale, we back-transformed the predicted values and confidence limits into probabilities for graphing and interpretation. We examined sensitivity of coyote abundance estimate precision (i.e., coeff. of variation [CV]) to reduced sampling effort by sequentially reducing the full 2010 capture-mark-recapture data set for the BFG study area and examining changes in CV relative to the estimate from the full data set. The full 2010 BFG data set consisted of 39 survey occasions (i.e., weeks) pooled into 3 biologically relevant seasons. We treated each of the 3 seasons as a single sampling occasion for closed-population abundance estimation purposes. We defined seasons as breeding (Jan-Apr), denning and pup-rearing (May-Jul), and dispersal (Aug-Dec). We treated multiple encounters of the same animal during the same season (i.e., detected in !1 week) as a single encounter. We subsampled the 39-occasion data set by randomly selecting a subset of occasions to retain in the reduced data set. We selected subsets of 15-35 sampling occasions, at 5 occasion intervals (i.e., 15, 20, etc.) and replicated the random selection process 100 times for each subsampling level. We used Program MARK (version 6.0; White and Burnham 1999) and the R package RMark (Laake 2013) to fit 3 closedpopulation capture-mark-recapture models to the full data set and each replicate data set for each subsampling level. The 3 models differed in how detection probability (p) was modeled (i.e., constant p over time, time-specific p, and constant p with additive behavioral effect). We derived a model-averaged abundance estimate and associated SE and CV for all data sets to account for model selection uncertainty (Burnham and Anderson 2003), and calculated the median of estimated CV values across all replicates within each subsampling level to assess changes in expected estimator precision associated with different survey effort levels.

We collected and analyzed a combined 434 scats from BFG and CC during February 2010-April 2012. We successfully species-typed 316 (73%) of these scats. Fifty four (17%) were from bobcats (Lynx rufus), 43 (14%) from gray fox (Urocyon cinereoargenteus), and 219 (69%) from coyotes. Of the 219 coyote scats, 136 (62%) yielded consensus genotypes representing 70 unique individuals.
The allelic dropout rate averaged 0.28 alleles/replicate across loci. This per-replicate error rate equated to the probability of a false homozygote in the consensus genotype of 0.28 2 /2 ¼ 3.9%. We constructed consensus genotypes from genotyping results at an average of 11.24 microsatellite loci. Probability of identity was 5.8 Â 10 À15 overall, and 6.4 Â 10 À6 for siblings using all 12 loci. The minimum number of loci from which a consensus genotype was constructed was 7. Probability of identity for 7 loci was 5.0 Â 10 À8 overall, and 9.4 Â 10 À4 for siblings (Gulsby et al. 2015).
The results of the logistic regression model evaluating the effect of season on genotyping success showed that spring, which had a positive effect on genotyping success, was the only informative parameter in the model. Parameter estimates for other seasons were also positive, but we cannot be certain of the magnitude and direction of their effect on genotyping success because their 95% confidence intervals included zero. Confidence intervals of the odds ratios for each season overlapped one another, but success appeared greater during spring (Table 1). The same trend was evident for the estimated seasonal probabilities of genotyping success, although uncertainty was relatively high. Specifically, the predicted probability of genotyping a confirmed coyote scat collected during spring (0.71) tended to be greater than for scats collected during summer (0.57), autumn (0.53), and winter (0.63; Fig. 2).
Estimator precision (CV) of model-averaged abundance for the full BFG 2010 data set was relatively high (CV < 0.15) and remained high (CV < 0.20) for the 35-and 30-week subsampling levels (Fig. 3). Precision rapidly decreased below acceptable levels (CV > 0.20) for data sets with <30 sampling occasions.

Fecal genotyping success is generally greater during cooler, drier periods, or in climates where those conditions are relatively common (Farrell et al. 2000, Lucchini et al. 2002, Nsubuga et al. 2004, Piggott 2004, Murphy et al. 2007). Thus, we expected our success rates would be significantly lower than those outside the humid subtropical climate of the Southeast. We successfully species-typed 73% of scats and constructed consensus genotypes for 62% of coyote scats. For comparison, species-typing was successful for !95% of scats collected in Utah, 88% in New Mexico, 80% in northern New York, and 60% in northern Virginia, USA (Kays et al. 2008, Panasci et al. 2011, Bozarth et al. 2015, Lonsinger et al. 2015). Consensus coyote genotypes were constructed for 80-90% (depending on season) of coyote scats in Utah, 53% in northern Virginia, 58% in western Virginia, 48% in California, and 36% in northern New York (Kohn et al. 1999, Kays et al. 2008, Bozarth et al. 2015, Lonsinger et al. 2015, Morin et al. 2016), although the number of markers used to construct genotypes varied considerably among these studies. Researchers in northeastern North Carolina, USA, an area with climatic conditions closely resembling those on our Georgia sites, constructed individual coyote or red wolf (Canis rufus) genotypes for 20% of collected scats (McVey et al. 2013). Our success was greater, with 31% of all scats collected yielding consensus coyote genotypes. Overall, we believe our success rates compared favorably to those of others, considering Georgia's climate. However, other variables such as scat preservation methods prior to DNA extraction also influence fecal genotyping success (Frantzen et al. 1998, Nsubuga et al. 2004), so some variation in success rates among studies is likely attributable to factors other than climatic conditions. Lonsinger et al. (2015) and Lucchini et al. (2002) reported PCR success was greater in cooler seasons, but fecal DNA degraded faster during winter in Australia, likely due to increased moisture during that season (Piggott 2004). We, therefore, hypothesized that samples collected during autumn, the season most closely resembling the cool, dry conditions conducive to preservation of fecal DNA on our sites, would have the greatest success rates. This hypothesis was not supported, although we found some evidence for increased success during spring. Alternately, seasonal differences in success rates may have been influenced more strongly by coyote diets than seasonal weather conditions. A concurrent study on our sites revealed that coyotes consumed significant quantities of blackberry (Rubus spp.) during summer, and muscadine (Vitis rotundifolia) and persimmon (Diospyros virginiana) during autumn (Kelly et al. 2015). These scats were composed primarily of undigested seeds; very little fecal material was present for sampling. Notably, our success rates trended lower during these seasons, although the differences did not differ statistically. Lack of fecal material available in scats composed primarily of similar food items impeded genotyping efforts in North Carolina (McVey et al. 2013). Others have also suggested a possible role of diet variation in genotyping success rates (Panasci et al. 2011, Lonsinger et al. 2015).  Solberg et al. ( 2006) recommended a 2.5-3:1 ratio of fecal samples to "assumed" animals in the population for abundance estimation. We analyzed 133 fecal samples from BFG during 2010 and an estimated 21 coyotes occupied the site during that year (Gulsby et al. 2015), meaning the ratio of samples to individual coyotes was 6.3:1. Precision of the abundance estimate (as indexed by CV) was adequate for detecting gross changes in coyote abundance and the subsampling exercise indicated estimates remained precise (i.e., 0.20), even with a 25% decrease in sampling effort. Although there is uncertainty in the relationship between sampling occasions and sample size on our sites, a 25% decrease in sampling effort would likely result in a ratio of samples to individuals still in excess of the heuristic suggested by Solberg et al. (2006). However, Solberg et al. (2006) successfully reached consensus genotypes for 70% of brown bear (Ursus arctos) scats collected in Sweden. Thus, in areas like ours where DNA degradation is exacerbated by environmental conditions, or scats from target versus nontarget species are more difficult to differentiate in the field, larger sample sizes are likely necessary. Another important consideration is relative abundance of target animals. In areas with relatively few coyotes, it may be necessary to increase the spatial and temporal scales of sampling to increase captures and achieve desired precision in abundance and demographic parameter estimates (Morin et al. 2016). Finally, the closed population models used in our analysis were relatively simplistic (e.g., no capture heterogeneity). Fitting of more complex models would presumably require even larger data sets (Laufenberg et al. 2013).
Reducing sampling frequency to periods >1 week would likely also increase the mean age of collected scats, decreasing sample quality. Panasci et al. (2011) noted 5-day-old scats contained DNA that was highly degraded compared with that of 1-day-old scats, and Santini et al. (2007) found significant degradation of DNA in scats older than 3 days. Therefore, those who wish to avoid continuous weekly sampling might reduce sampling effort by conducting weekly sampling only during certain periods of the year, instead of decreasing sampling frequency. Alternately, subjective estimation of scat age via inspection of moisture content and degree of decomposition might be used to avoid sampling older scats. However, accurate visual estimation of canid scat age has proven difficult (Piggott 2004).
Overall, we believe our results are encouraging for the future applicability of fecal genotyping to estimate abundance and demography of coyotes or other species in the Southeast. Despite unfavorable conditions for preservation of fecal DNA, our success rates and precision of resulting estimates of N (measured in terms of CV) were sufficient for detecting gross changes in coyote abundance, and provide a starting point for those proposing similar work. Although these results can be somewhat generalized to other areas, conducting a pilot study to establish baseline information for a population of interest is an important step in developing a robust and reliable survey design.
Cost of an adequate survey to accomplish research objectives or inform management decisions is a common concern. Total cost of genotyping the 434 samples was approximately US$20,000 ($46/sample). We chose not to estimate costs associated with sample collection, because this process is undoubtedly affected by a variety of sitespecific factors such as area sampled, animal density, and difficulty of travel along survey routes, which should be accounted for during creation of the research budget and experimental design. Despite these concerns, the precise coyote abundance estimates typically afforded by fecal genotyping are likely justified in situations where results are used to inform expensive management decisions or research findings.
